unit.why: A short anecdote quoted from another book: the Apta Rav as a youth fasted, asked R. Elimelech about it, and received a pointed answer. It is embedded in an ethical discussion against fasting.
unit.boundary_note: Part of a running anthology of quotations against fasting; the previous and next divisions are teachings on the same theme.

stories.start_quote: והרב מאפטא סיפר לי שבילדותו היה מתענה
stories.summary_en: The Apta Rav recounts that as a youth he fasted and asked R. Elimelech, who allowed fasting only if he could then eat a kvart of dry kasha, and who said that with two more partners he would abolish fasts altogether.

tags.why: The whole anecdote concerns the youth's fasting and the rebbe's criticism of it.
Debate over whether ascetic self-denial is proper.

quotes: ושאל להרב ר׳ אלימלך זצ״ל ע״ז
tags.why: A disciple consults his master about his devotional practice.
The tale is framed as told by a named tsaddik to the author.

quotes: וכשם שמצוה לשמור ישראל מעבירה כן מצוה ליזהר
tags.why: The anecdote is wrapped in an ethical and halakhic exhortation against fasting.
The rebbe permits fasting only under a condition; the frame enjoins the weak not to fast.

quotes: שהוא ד׳ לוגין אז מותר לך להתענות
tags.why: The ruling is phrased in quasi-halakhic terms of measure and permission.

quotes: לאכול אין מלכות קווארט קאשי יבישה
tags.why: The kvart of dry kasha may be a witty, hyperbolic condition.
Illustrates R. Elimelech's teaching on moderation, though it is more doctrine than virtue.

missing_concepts: opposition to fasting / anti-asceticism as Hasidic doctrine
guarding one's bodily strength in divine service
